title: The Morning Brief: College Bans Collide With Court Orders as August 31 Looms
dek: The Big Ten and SEC have issued immediate eligibility bans on players with professional experience, directly contradicting a Louisiana court order allowing some of those same athletes to return. The collision between institutional and judicial authority will test itself in three days.
author: GoCheckMySports
key_fact: College conferences and a state court are now in direct conflict over player eligibility, with the August 31 injunction hearing and concurrent NFL roster cutdowns likely to generate more players seeking court relief and clarify whether judicial orders can override conference rules.
bottom_line: College conferences and a state court are now in direct legal conflict over player eligibility, with conference bans issued Tuesday and Tuesday night directly contradicting a Louisiana court order from last week. The August 31 injunction hearing and concurrent NFL roster cutdowns will test whether judicial orders can override conference rules and will likely generate additional players seeking court relief. The NFL approved a league-record $9.612 billion Seahawks sale and ended the Pro Bowl after 80 years of declining viewership. Training-camp injuries are reshaping rosters across football and basketball as the regular season approaches.
body: The Big Ten and SEC have moved to exclude players with professional experience from college competition, but they are colliding head-on with a Louisiana court order that explicitly permits certain NFL-affiliated athletes to return. The desk reported yesterday that a state court issued a temporary restraining order allowing players who participated in NFL training camp and preseason to rejoin college rosters, ruling that those athletes would not have entered the professional process had they known college eligibility would remain available. On Tuesday and Tuesday night, the Big Ten voted unanimously and the SEC announced identical football rules, plus basketball prohibitions on NBA and WNBA experience, effective immediately. That timing creates a direct legal confrontation: players who hold court orders allowing their return now face conference bans from the institutions they wish to play for.

The Big Ten's rule prohibits football players who have signed professional contracts, appeared on professional rosters at any point, or declared for the NFL Draft as underclassmen without withdrawing. The SEC extends the same football prohibition to men's and women's basketball players with NBA and WNBA experience. Both leagues acted in direct response to the Louisiana court's order, according to the desk's reporting, but the orders they issued contradict that judicial ruling rather than comply with it.

The drivers are institutional: the conferences want to maintain eligibility boundaries and prevent professional athletes from returning to college. The honest read is that the reporting does not explain why the conferences chose to issue immediate bans knowing litigation was pending, or what legal counsel advised about enforcing rules against court orders. What is clear is that the August 31 injunction hearing will test whether a state court can force conferences to accept players they have banned, and whether the NFL roster cutdowns that same day generate additional players seeking court relief.

Beyond the eligibility collision, the week absorbed significant business and personnel moves. The NFL owners voted unanimously to ratify the $9.612 billion sale of the Seattle Seahawks to a group led by venture capitalist Vinod Khosla's family, the largest franchise transaction in league history and a 59 percent increase over the previous record, the $6.05 billion Commanders purchase in 2023. The deal is expected to close in September. The league also ended its nearly 80-year Pro Bowl competition, replacing the televised all-star game with a recognition-only honor bestowed on 88 selected players. Viewership had collapsed from 6.7 million in 2023 to 1.9 million in 2026, according to the desk's reporting, prompting the shift.

On the field, training camp injuries are reshaping rosters ahead of the regular season. Giants slot receiver Calvin Austin suffered what was described as a serious knee injury without contact during Tuesday practice, buckling his knee while running a route against cornerback Deonte Banks. No official diagnosis has been provided, and the full severity remains unclear. The Ravens placed center Danny Pinter on injured reserve after he tore his patellar tendon during a joint practice with Minnesota, sidelining him for the entire 2026 season. Pinter had signed with Baltimore this offseason and was competing to be the starting center. The Aces' forward NaLyssa Smith will miss the remainder of the regular season after suffering a non-contact leg injury in Sunday's win over Toronto with five games remaining. Smith had been leading the WNBA in field goal percentage at 63.8% and averaging 11.7 points and 6.4 rebounds.

In basketball, the Fever-Sky game on NBC and Peacock drew 3.31 million viewers, the most-watched WNBA regular-season game since opening weekend 1997. Chicago won 113-90, with Caitlin Clark and Kelsey Mitchell combining for 67 points. The game drew attention not only for its ratings but also for an incident late in the third quarter when former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom was ejected after a verbal altercation with Sky guard Natasha Cloud. The Chicago Sky has placed an indefinite ban on Freedom attending home games. The desk reported that accounts of the confrontation differ: Sky owner Michael Alter characterized it as Freedom stepping forward as a threat after Cloud made a layup, while courtside fan Trista Smith stated Freedom did not initiate the altercation. A league source indicated that Freedom is not banned from attending other WNBA games and the league does not intend a league-wide ban.

In the NFL, Packers running back Josh Jacobs has been charged with misdemeanor battery and misdemeanor criminal damage to property following his May arrest in Wisconsin. The Brown County District Attorney declined to pursue a felony strangulation charge and two other misdemeanors, narrowing the charge slate from the original arrest.

In soccer, Liverpool reached an outline agreement with Paris Saint-Germain on winger Bradley Barcola's transfer valued at approximately 120 million pounds, comprising just over 100 million pounds guaranteed plus 20 million pounds in performance-based add-ons. The compromise fee represents a significant reduction from PSG's initial 145 million pound valuation. The deal's completion raises questions about the future of Cody Gakpo at Anfield, though the reporting does not specify the nature of those doubts.

In baseball, MLB formally proposed a restricted free-agency window with a December 21 signing deadline followed by a month-long transaction freeze, aiming to create NFL- and NBA-style offseason urgency. The proposal also includes reduced injured-list minimums and expanded Rule 5 Draft eligibility but is conditioned on a salary cap system the players union immediately rejected as harmful to player compensation. MLBPA interim executive director Bruce Meyer stated the salary cap demand would drastically reduce overall player compensation and eliminate fully guaranteed contracts through escrow.
In track, Brazil's Alison dos Santos ran 45.80 seconds in the 400m hurdles at the Diamond League final in Zurich, breaking the world record.
